I’m 51 years old and I’ve been farming these eight mu in Quzhou County my whole life. My father taught me, and I’ve kept up with what the neighbors and the extension agents say. Around here, the land is good but the growing season is tight, so the only sensible system is the wheat-maize rotation: winter wheat planted in October and harvested early June, then summer maize planted right after and harvested before the next wheat sowing. I’m not going to gamble with new crops I don’t know—cotton prices have been unstable and vegetables need too much labor and market access. I’ll stick with what works.

My winter wheat is already in the ground. I sowed **Luyuan 502**, an improved variety that yields well and resists lodging. I rotary-tilled before sowing and applied a compound fertilizer as basal. This spring I’ll top-dress with urea at green-up and jointing, irrigate four times (returning green, jointing, booting, and grain filling), and spray for aphids, powdery mildew, and weeds—about four pesticide applications in total. I expect around 1,000 jin per mu, maybe a bit more if the weather cooperates.

After wheat harvest in early June, I’ll sow **Deng Hai 605**, a hybrid maize seed. There’s no time to plough again, so I’ll use no-tillage direct seeding right into the wheat stubble. Maize needs less irrigation than wheat—two good flood irrigations, one at the jointing stage and one at filling, should be enough if the summer rains are normal. I’ll fertilize with compound and urea, and spray two to three times for corn borer and weeds. Hybrid maize usually gives me about 1,100 jin per mu.

This is my plan for the year.
